questions.q: How do I start adopting AI in my business?
questions.a: Start with a problem that's already costing you time or money, such as repetitive customer questions or slow review replies. Once you know the bottleneck, you can look for a tool that fixes it. Picking the technology first tends to produce pilots that test shiny tools and change very little.

questions.q: Which tasks should a multi-location business automate first?
questions.a: Look for work that's repetitive, data-heavy and easy to measure. Good first candidates are sorting customer feedback into themes or urgency levels, flagging locations whose reviews are slipping, and sending personalized post-visit surveys. These are low risk, and you can see quickly whether they're working.

questions.q: How long should an AI pilot run?
questions.a: A pilot of 4–6 weeks across 3–5 locations gives you enough data to judge the results. Record your baseline metrics first, such as response time, CSAT and review volume, so you have something to compare against. Then track performance, team feedback and time saved before deciding whether to scale.

questions.q: What should I look for in an AI tool?
questions.a: Choose a tool that plugs into the systems you already use, such as your CRM, ordering or survey tools. It should handle multi-location workflows and permissions, and its reporting should point to actions your team can take. A dashboard nobody acts on adds little value.

questions.q: How do I get my team to use AI?
questions.a: Explain what's changing, train people on how the AI supports their work, and show them how to act on its recommendations. Share insights with store managers and regional leads as well as HQ. Teams adopt AI when it makes their day easier, so simple outputs like a weekly list of top action items work well.

questions.q: What does predictive AI add once automation is running?
questions.a: Predictive AI helps you spot problems before they show up in your results. It can forecast a drop in CSAT, highlight service issues trending in a region and flag customers who are likely to churn. That shifts your team's question from what happened to what you should do next.
